extracted.intended_audience: public administrators, UIC (unemployment insurance commission) officials, policy makers and staff responsible for claimant communications and procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how an unemployment insurance authority should inform claimants and the public — covering pamphlets, audio-visuals, language access, duties to inform, access to legal rules, participation and appeal procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement guarantees for administrative decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative decisions must be backed by guarantees that they will be carried out by the individuals concerned; administrative authorities must have the means to recover money paid out illegally and may make use of penalties when illegality results from deliberate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure effective recovery mechanisms for unlawfully paid benefits and, where appropriate, penalties; recognize that coercive measures raise special procedural problems (see Chapter 14 {Enforcing the decision}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of rules / Right to understand
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizen wants to be informed of the reasons for and machinery of administrative actions that affect him, of his rights, of the avenues of appeal open to him and of the exact extent of his obligations; access to legislation, regulations and caselaw is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate access to sources of rules even before decision-making commences; explain progress of the process, what is expected of claimants, stages of decision-making; ensure good initial contact, direct contact with officials, and written notification of reasons (see Chapter 9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation / convergent procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should be associated with the decision-making process via a 'convergent procedure' that enables them to express their own view and contribute to the decision affecting their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve access problems before dialogue can begin: provide access to the administrative authority and decision-maker (in person when feasible), access to the case file, machinery for ongoing input where cooperation is needed after decisions, and dispute procedures that guarantee a real possibility of making views prevail before review authorities (see Chapter 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avenues of appeal — accessibility and quality of review
rubrics_metrics.description: There must exist an avenue of appeal against administrative decisions (typically before administrative tribunals) structured so that access is easy and requires a minimum of formality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design review authorities to enhance impartiality and technical competence; ensure review decisions are of high quality and command respect from both administrative authorities and the public (see Chapter 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlet presentation and visual design
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlets should be attractively presented without being luxurious; graphics should aid understanding rather than being purely decorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a few descriptive drawings (with humour where applicable) rather than purely decorative photographs; ensure consistent, successful typography and layout across pamphlets (noting that some pamphlets like 'Rights and Obligations' and 'How to Complete Your Claimant's Report' could be improved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlet style and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlet text should be clear, simplified and explain technical terminology so it is understandable by the public; terminological consistency is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid terminological inconsistency in official documents; ensure translations are comprehensible (French/English versions must convey the same meaning); prefer clear, direct language (the French version of 'Appeal Procedure' was noted as heavy and unclear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlet content completeness and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Informational pamphlets must not be merely incomplete or over-simplified; they must provide claimants with sufficient information to fulfil essential roles (e.g., applications, claimant reports, job search obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state consequences and applicable penalties for failure to perform obligations (rather than vague allusions); adequately emphasize the obligation to search actively for employment; include essential cross-referenced information (e.g., prior approval requirements for training allowances) so key points are not scattered across many pamphlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading analogies and state statutory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should avoid analogies (e.g., equating unemployment insurance with contractual insurance) that create misconceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a requirement is regulatory or statutory in nature (e.g., Active Job Search Program), cite the specific wording of the Act and Regulations, state the true purpose plainly, and remind claimants of consequences of noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and consolidation of informational materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider consolidating multiple pamphlets into a single information manual or separate manuals for insured employees and claimants to avoid scattering essential information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a single manual, arrange contents under logical subject headings with detailed, easy-to-use table of contents and cross-references; keep material presentation modest; a well-written manual can serve as a permanent guide and training tool for staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio-visual content suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio-visual displays are particularly suited to conveying simple, clear and concise information and should put a limited number of key concepts across in simple, direct language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include humour where applicable; improve visual components (animated cartoons preferable to banal still photographs) to better engage viewers; limit content to core concepts given complexity of the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio-visual distribution and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The usefulness of audio-visual techniques depends on their distribution and the availability of equipment in offices; consider wider public-education placements beyond the point of claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide displays in many offices or use display booths in shopping/community centres, TV/radio spots, and short cinema features; evaluate whether the claimant's reporting moment is the best time for general information; anticipate cost but note medium-term savings from reduced misunderstandings and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-official languages for informational material
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish key explanatory pamphlets (e.g., 'Rights and Obligations' and 'How to Complete Your Claimant's Report') in non-official languages commonly used by immigrant communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden distribution of translated pamphlets where the composition of clientele warrants it, to make general publicity accessible to main language groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions about translating legal forms and discrimination risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Application forms and claimant reports are statutory documents with legal effects; printing them in other languages raises issues (Official Languages Act, discrimination, inconsistency with subsequent official-language notices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh risks: (1) discrimination inherent in choosing which non-official languages to print, (2) illogicality of receiving later notices only in an official language, (3) likelihood that bilingual intermediaries exist; proceed cautiously and consider legal/institutional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal communication — employee language skills and interpreting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on friends as interpreters is often inadequate; the authority should develop and deploy employees with language skills to interview claimants in commonly encountered non-official languages where warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign and train Agents I and II and BCOs in non-official languages frequently encountered in particular areas to ensure direct contact and accurate communication; be mindful of issues raised by official bilingualism policies but adapt to local needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory duty to inform (proposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative authority should be required by statute to disseminate to the public the general information needed by those employed in insurable employment who wish to take advantage of their entitlement to benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed wording (example): '105A The Commission shall undertake such measures of publicity as it deems appropriate in order to inform insured persons and their employers of the provisions of this Act.' Consider whether the Act should also require individualized information to claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to legal rules — clarity and findability
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of the Act and the Regulations is currently difficult to understand and difficult to find; style of drafting and scattering of Regulations impede public access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reorganization, clarification and simplification of the Act and Regulations (especially procedural provisions) so that the legal rules can be used directly by non-lawyers; avoid antiquated drafting conventions that prevent direct public use of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative consolidation and publication of statutes/regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce and publish an 'administrative consolidation' (an updated edition) of the Act and Regulations to improve accessibility and convenience for employers, employees and the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An up-to-date consolidated text would assist both the public and the administration; failure to publish such a consolidation (noted since 1971) hinders access to legal rules.
